r6-m02.abandon: The mechanism says the cued base's extra losses at T 1.0 are tail-token slips, and that a lower temperature would avoid them. The board already contradicts that cause. (1) result-faf15a located the first wrong step in 51 finished-wrong T 1.0 answers of the cued base and found that 'the base's wrong step is not an unlikely sample'. Those steps score 'log-prob -0.53 per token vs -0.63 for control text (W4 refuted)'. The item concludes: 'truncation or low temperature cannot remove these steps, which fits the min-p/top-p negatives'. A tail-token slip would score below control text, and lowering T or cutting the tail would remove it. (2) result-44b4df cut the tail directly at T 1.0 and found 'No truncation rule beats untruncated sampling on MATH-500 at T 1.0': 'base top-p 0.95 -0.2 [-3.8, 3.2]' and 'base min-p 0.1 -1.2 pts [-4.6, 2.2]'. The tail-slip cause predicts a gain there, at least on short problems where loops do not return. (3) The observation the mechanism was built to explain has a simpler reading. In knowledge-13cff3, 'on the 402 problems that finish at T 0.6, T 1.0 gets 361-364 against 378'. That subset is chosen by the T 0.6 sample's own outcome: its finished answers are '94 %' right. Selecting on T 0.6's own outcome favours T 0.6 even when both temperatures have the same per-problem accuracy, so the number does not show a second item axis or a short-problem crossover. The mechanism's cause is contradicted, and its target fact is explained by selection, so a theory built on it would waste tests.

r6-m03.abandon: The mechanism says the top-8 directions carry only a commit-and-stop policy that cuts cap hits and 'do[es] nothing about accuracy'. The board already contradicts this. (1) result-284db5, the item the mechanism starts from, reports a direction-specific accuracy gain for top-8 on hard328 with the cue: 'top-8 minus base +8.5 [4.3, 12.8]', 'top-8 minus random +10.4 pts [5.8, 14.9]', and 'Top-8 solves 30 of the 49 problems only RL solved'. That item concludes that 'the 8 directions are more than the cue'. (2) Stopping alone cannot produce that gain. result-51fd20 shows that on the same 328 problems, making the cued base commit early loses points: 'its cap hits on the 328 are failures to solve, not failures to stop', and 'Of the 77 stored cap hits a forced commit is right on 0-2 at every N'. So turning top-8's 31 fewer cap hits (77 -> 46) into answers by stopping would add at most about 2 right, not the +28 observed (164 -> 192). Most of top-8's gain is therefore error reduction, the job the mechanism gives only to the bulk. (3) Top-8 also does not act like a pure commit policy in its text. result-284db5: 'with top-8, Wait/perhaps/Hmm rates rise to RL's level', so it adds RL's hesitation habit instead of halting sooner. (4) On MATH-500, result-36e8cd reports 'base + those 8 directions plain 427 vs matched random 197 (+46.0 [40.8, 51.0])', and result-d2933e reports 88 vs a 'matched random rank-8 control 36' at n=100. These are accuracy gains far above a matched control, though the plain prompt mixes in the cue's effect. The split 'top-8 = stopping without accuracy, bulk = accuracy without stopping' is therefore contradicted by result-284db5 together with result-51fd20. The facts the mechanism leans on (22 quick finished-wrong top-8 answers against the cued base's 13, and RL minus top-8 hitting the cap 90 times) are side effects next to a measured accuracy gain from top-8, not evidence that top-8 adds no accuracy.

r6-m07.abandon: The mechanism explains the base's excess of 0-of-4 problems as base-specific misreading attractors that RL removes. Three of the items it starts from contradict each link of that chain. (1) The excess is not base-specific: RL is lumpier than the base. result-e41d94 reports "but 8 (base) and 12 (RL) more 0-of-4 problems than binomial". If RL removed the attractors behind the excess, RL's own 0-of-4 excess would shrink, not grow. (2) The base's 0-of-4 problems fail by wrong plans, not misreads. result-afc423: "Base items with a right sibling: 39 of 48 slip/misread/format; without (base 0/4): 8 of 12 wrong plan." Misreads and slips sit on problems the base sometimes solves, which is where independent slips belong. They do not sit on the lumpy 0-of-4 problems. (3) RL's lower misread rate does not reach wrong plans. result-faf15a: "RL lowers misreadings and slips, not wrong plans" (Math 3.1 by label: "misread -1.52, slip -0.72, wrong plan +0.03"). Consistent with that, result-afc423 finds "of the 33 base-0/4 problems RL has 0/4 on 16", so about half the lumpy problems persist under RL. So the 1.52-nat drop in misreads cannot be what removes the base's 0-of-4 clusters. The clustering is a shared, plan-level difficulty that both models show, which is the reading r4-m07's refutation in knowledge-90431f also leaves open ("35 of 131 RL wrong answers equal a base wrong answer"). A test of answer agreement across base prompts would measure answer repetition on problems whose errors the board already labels as wrong plans, not misread attractors.

r6-m08.abandon: The mechanism says the base fails between problems because it settles on a length budget from the prompt that is too small, so it writes a short, compressed answer where RL writes a long one. The board items say the opposite: the base's failures are long answers, and its failures on one problem are sporadic, which a budget fixed by the prompt cannot produce. (1) result-5e17a6: 'Base answers <= 2,000 tokens: 263, 13 wrong'. Short base answers are about 95 % right, so at most 13 of the base's 63 finished-wrong MATH-500 answers can be short. Its hand labels of the 65 RL-only problems name '14 misread, 14 arithmetic/algebra slip' and '16 cap hits with no loop', and none is a truncated or compressed solution. (2) result-f21d2e: 'no J-lens feature predicts a wrong base answer better than length (AUROC length 0.831'. Together with (1) this means longer base answers are the wrong ones. Under the mechanism, base length would be a weak or reversed predictor of failure. (3) result-afc423: '81% of the 198-sample gap (4 samples per problem' lies in problems the base solves at least once, and 'Cell base 3/4 -> RL 4/4: 86 problems = 43% of the gap'. A budget fixed by the prompt is shared by every sample of a problem, so the right siblings show the budget was big enough. The facts entry for r5-m02 also shows the wrong siblings run longer (+0.19 log ratio), not shorter. At most the 19 % in base-0/4 problems is left for the mechanism. (4) result-a6ab7a: 'Base fails RL prefixes mostly by cap hit (34 of 48 wrong at 50 %)'. Even when RL's long plan is handed to it, the base fails by running past the cap, not by stopping early. (5) result-51fd20: 'its cap hits on the 328 are failures to solve, not failures to stop', and 'the tokens between 8,000 and 16,384 buy 12 problems'. The base loses problems when it is cut short and wins problems by writing long. (6) The observation the mechanism was built on does not support it. result-b30f15's probe at the last prompt token predicts 'sample is in the largest group of agreeing answers' across problems at 0.73-0.77. That is problem difficulty, which also drives length up, not a short length budget. The proposed first test conditions on finished answers in RL-length quartiles, but the items above already place the base's errors on its long answers, inside the same problems where shorter siblings succeed.

r6-m09.abandon: m09 says the 3.0 RL-Zero releases learned to commit by about 12k tokens: on long problems they 'finish anyway and guess, rather than continuing or hitting the cap'. Two board items measure the 3.0 releases directly and show the opposite, that they keep going and hit the length limit. (1) knowledge-9f8067 reports, from a third-party leaderboard (LiveCodeBench v6, T 0.8 / top-p 0.95, 32,768 tokens): "3.0 Code 13.8 % (64 % of rollouts loop)". Code 3.0 is the model whose few MATH-500 cap hits m09 was built to explain. On its own training domain, with a cap well past 12k, most of its rollouts loop instead of committing. (2) knowledge-b15a21 quotes 2610.30882 on Olmo-3-7B (3.0) RL-Zero-Math: "RL-Zero-Math 76.5/1k at T 0.6 with 29.1% length-limit hits vs 17.8% base". The 3.0 Math release hits the length limit more often than the base. A commit-by-12k habit predicts fewer limit hits than the base. Consistent with this, knowledge-8a31ad reports that the 3.0 Math model scores only 75.0 on MATH-500 at T 0.6 with a 31,744 cap, far below the 448/500 it scores at T 1.0 (result-edceef). That is the pattern of a model that runs long at cool settings, not one that stops by 12k. Code 3.0's 5 cap hits on MATH-500 at T 1.0 fit a model that simply writes short answers on a domain it was not trained on (3,069 tokens per problem, result-edceef). They do not show a 12k commit habit learned from masked truncations, because both 3.0 releases run to the cap whenever the setting allows it. The first test (finished-row length share in fr-01 F_math500) would therefore test a habit the board already contradicts.

r6-m12.abandon: The only evidence for the mechanism is that the base's 'Answer:' answers are more accurate overall: result-fdc8da, "'Answer:' line median -8.36 (n=132, 121 right)", against roughly 289 of 338 boxed answers right. The same item splits the base's quick wrong answers by marker, and that split goes the other way. It reports "wrong answers under 4,000 tokens median -0.53 (n=21)" and says "RL gives a wrong box the base's probability (median D 0.001, n=10)". Only about 10 of the roughly 49 wrong boxed answers are boxed answers under 4,000 tokens. That leaves about 11 quick wrong answers that are not boxed. Only about 30 finished rows carry neither marker, so at least 8 of those 11 must be 'Answer:' answers. In other words, most of the 11 wrong 'Answer:' answers are quick ones. 'Answer:' answers are at most 132 of the roughly 350 quick answers (about 0.38; result-5e17a6 counts "Base answers <= 2,000 tokens: 263, 13 wrong."). Yet they make up about half of the 21 quick wrong answers. So among quick answers, 'Answer:' answers are wrong at least as often as boxed ones (about 9 % vs about 4 %). The boxed answers' extra errors are almost all long answers on hard problems. So the overall 'Answer:' advantage comes from which problems each marker lands on (difficulty and length), not from a less accurate boxed register at matched difficulty. A further point against reading the marker as a register: knowledge-8229be finds that boxing goes together with higher accuracy, not lower. In every arm that recovers accuracy, "Every arm that recovers accuracy also takes RL's format and length: 'Answer:' line in 0-4 % of answers vs 39-46 % for base-like arms". RL itself boxes in 100 % of answers (knowledge-499152: "'Answer:' line share base 0.44, RL 0.00"). So a large boxed share cannot be part of the cue-to-RL gap. The mechanism's first test (a within-quartile difference of at least +5 points) is therefore expected to fail, and building predictions on it would waste the tests.
